questions.stem: A 48-year-old man presents with severe chest pain and is diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction. Laboratory tests reveal elevated troponin levels, and an echocardiogram shows decreased ejection fraction. A biopsy of the affected myocardium reveals cell swelling, disruption of cellular membranes, and the release of intracellular contents into the surrounding tissue. Which of the following findings most specifically indicates necrosis rather than apoptosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Cell shrinkage with intact cell membrane

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Inflammatory response in surrounding tissue

 

Necrosis is a form of cell death that typically results from acute injury, such as ischemia during a myocardial infarction. In necrosis, cell membrane integrity is lost, leading to the release of intracellular contents into the extracellular space. This process triggers an inflammatory response in the surrounding tissue, which is a hallmark feature of necrosis. In the case of myocardial infarction, necrosis results from oxygen deprivation in the heart muscle, leading to the death of cells and subsequent inflammation.

 

Apoptosis, on the other hand, is a controlled, programmed form of cell death that typically does not elicit an inflammatory response because the cell contents remain contained within intact membranes. The body's immune system usually does not react to apoptosis as it does to necrosis. Therefore, the presence of an inflammatory response is the key feature that indicates necrosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chromatin condensation and nuclear fragmentation: These changes are characteristic of apoptosis, not necrosis. During apoptosis, the cell undergoes controlled dismantling, which includes chromatin condensation and nuclear fragmentation. These processes are orderly and do not result in the loss of cell membrane integrity or an inflammatory response.

 

Option B. Cell shrinkage with intact cell membrane: Cell shrinkage with an intact membrane is another feature of apoptosis. In apoptosis, cells contract, and their membranes remain intact, preventing the release of intracellular contents and avoiding inflammation. This is in contrast to necrosis, where the cell membrane is disrupted.

 

Option D. Activation of caspases: Caspases are enzymes that play a critical role in the initiation and execution of apoptosis. Their activation leads to the systematic dismantling of the cell during apoptosis. In necrosis, however, caspase activation is not typically involved, and the process is far more chaotic and results in cell lysis and inflammation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Necrosis, unlike apoptosis, is characterized by the loss of cell membrane integrity and the release of intracellular contents, leading to an inflammatory response in surrounding tissue. This is a key distinguishing feature of necrosis.

 




ore, the presence of an inflammatory response is the key feature that indicates necrosis.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents due to recurrent ear infections, chronic diarrhea, and eczema. On examination, he has small bruises and petechiae on his skin. Laboratory findings reveal a low platelet count and normal levels of white blood cells and red blood cells. Which of the following is the likely additional finding in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Family history of a maternal uncle who had a similar disorder

options.label: B
options.text: Family history of females affected more than males

options.label: C
options.text: Family history of disease exclusively transmitted from mother to all her progeny

options.label: D
options.text: Family history of at least 1 member in every previous generation affected irrespective of sex

questions.answerText: Family history of a maternal uncle who had a similar disorder
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Family history of a maternal uncle who had a similar disorder

 

The combination of recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), eczema, and a family history of bleeding disorders in males suggests Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS), an X-linked recessive condition. WAS is characterized by three primary features: immunodeficiency (leading to recurrent infections), thrombocytopenia (which leads to easy bruising and petechiae), and eczema.

 

In an X-linked recessive disorder like WAS, males are predominantly affected because they have only one X chromosome. If they inherit the defective gene, they manifest the disease. Female carriers typically do not exhibit symptoms because they have a second, healthy X chromosome. The description of a maternal uncle who died from a bleeding disorder is consistent with the X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, as the gene would have been passed from the mother, who may be an asymptomatic carrier.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Family history of females affected more than males: This pattern suggests an X-linked dominant inheritance or an autosomal dominant condition with sex-specific expression, neither of which applies here. In Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, males are affected more than females, as females are typically carriers due to the X-linked recessive nature of the disorder.

 

Option C. Family history of disease exclusively transmitted from mother to all her progeny: This pattern is characteristic of mitochondrial inheritance, where the condition is transmitted solely through the mother and affects both male and female progeny. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is not a mitochondrial disorder; it follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.

 

Option D. Family history of at least one member in every previous generation affected irrespective of sex: This pattern is typical of autosomal dominant inheritance, where males and females are equally likely to be affected. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome does not follow this pattern, as it affects males disproportionately due to its X-linked recessive nature.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia, and eczema, with a family history that typically involves male relatives, such as a maternal uncle, who may have died young due to a bleeding disorder.

 

Genetics:

 

  • X-linked recessive
  • Mutation in WASP gene
  • Affects only males
  • Carrier females are asymptomatic
  • Family history often shows affected maternal uncles (i.e., mother’s brother)

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is correctly matched?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1-B, 2-A, 3-D, 4-C

 

 

This question involves matching lymphomas with their characteristic clinical presentations. Let's break down each lymphoma and its corresponding clinical presentation:

 

  1. Hodgkin lymphoma - Classically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, making the correct match 1-B. Patients with Hodgkin lymphoma typically have swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and the disease often progresses slowly.
  2. Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) - This is an aggressive lymphoma that can present as a rapidly growing mass, often seen in areas like the Waldeyer ring (a ring of lymphoid tissue in the throat), which corresponds to 2-A.
  3. Burkitt lymphoma - An extremely aggressive form of lymphoma, often presenting in children and is associated with a rapidly growing mass in the jaw or mandible (especially in endemic areas like Africa). This matches 3-D.
  4. Mantle cell lymphoma - This type of lymphoma is associated with gastrointestinal involvement, where patients may present with GI polyps. Therefore, the correct match is 4-C.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Each type of lymphoma has specific clinical presentations that can help in their diagnosis. Key points to remember:

 

  • Hodgkin lymphoma presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy.
  • Diffuse large B cell lymphoma often presents as a rapid-growing mass at the Waldeyer ring.
  • Burkitt lymphoma presents as a rapidly growing mass affecting the mandible.
  • Mantle cell lymphoma is associated with GI polyps.


ore, the correct match is 4-C.

questions.stem: Which of the following kidney disorders is associated with a mutation in the COL4A5 chain?

options.label: A
options.text: A 45-year-old male presents with hematuria, proteinuria, and hearing loss

options.label: B
options.text: A 30-year-old female complains of shortness of breath and cough, and chest X-ray reveals pulmonary hemorrhage

options.label: C
options.text: A 25-year-old female undergoes renal biopsy showing thinning of glomerular basement membrane

options.label: D
options.text: A 50-year-old male presents with nephrotic syndrome and renal biopsy reveals nodular lesions in glomeruli.

questions.answerText: A 45-year-old male presents with hematuria, proteinuria, and hearing loss
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A 45-year-old male presents with hematuria, proteinuria, and hearing loss

 

The COL4A5 gene encodes a component of type IV collagen, which is critical in the structure of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). A mutation in COL4A5 is characteristic of Alport syndrome, a hereditary disorder that primarily affects the kidneys, eyes, and ears. Individuals with Alport syndrome often present with hematuria (blood in urine) and proteinuria (protein in urine), along with hearing loss due to defects in collagen in the inner ear. As this genetic disorder progresses, patients may develop chronic kidney disease and eventual kidney failure.

 

The description of a 45-year-old male with hematuria, proteinuria, and hearing loss aligns with the clinical manifestations of Alport syndrome, specifically linked to a mutation in the COL4A5 gene.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. A 30-year-old female complains of shortness of breath and cough, and chest X-ray reveals pulmonary hemorrhage: This scenario suggests Goodpasture syndrome, an autoimmune disease characterized by pulmonary hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. Goodpasture syndrome is associated with antibodies against type IV collagen, but it involves the alpha-3 chain of collagen (COL4A3), not COL4A5.

 

Option C. A 25-year-old female undergoes renal biopsy showing thinning of glomerular basement membrane: This presentation is more consistent with Thin Basement Membrane Nephropathy (TBMN), also known as benign familial hematuria. It is a condition characterized by a thinning of the glomerular basement membrane but is not linked to mutations in COL4A5.

 

Option D. A 50-year-old male presents with nephrotic syndrome and renal biopsy reveals nodular lesions in glomeruli: This describes diabetic nephropathy or nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease), which is common in patients with diabetes. It is not related to mutations in the COL4A5 gene.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Alport syndrome is associated with a mutation in the COL4A5 gene and presents with hematuria, proteinuria, and sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old female presents with recurrent abdominal pain and melena. Physical examination reveals multiple pigmented macules on her lips, buccal mucosa, and fingers. An upper endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the stomach and small intestine. The genetic testing confirms a mutation in the STK11 gene. Which of the following complications is she at greatest risk for?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Intussusception

 

The clinical presentation described in the question, including pigmented macules on the lips, buccal mucosa, and fingers combined with hamartomatous polyps in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, along with an STK11 gene mutation, is consistent with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS). This is a rare, autosomal dominant genetic disorder.

 

Polyps, Pigmentation, Positive family history help in diagnosis as STK11 mutations may be missing in some patients.  PJ Disease: Pigmentation, Jejunal polyps Dominant. 

 

The hallmark of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is the development of hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract, which can cause intussusception, a condition where a segment of the intestine folds into another section, leading to obstruction. Intussusception is the most immediate and significant risk in children and young adults with PJS due to the presence of large polyps, particularly in the small intestine.

 

Melanotic pigmentation can be seen in Addison disease, hemochromatosis, fibrous dysplasia of bone (Albright syndrome).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Colorectal cancer: Patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are indeed at an increased lifetime risk of developing various malignancies, including colorectal cancer. However, this risk typically increases in later adulthood, whereas intussusception is a more immediate concern in younger individuals.

 

Option B. Breast cancer: While women with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are at higher risk of developing breast cancer, this typically becomes a concern later in life. The primary concern in a 16-year-old with this syndrome is GI complications like intussusception.

 

Option C. Pancreatic cancer: Individuals with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are also at an increased risk of pancreatic cancer, but similar to colorectal and breast cancers, the risk of pancreatic cancer generally becomes significant later in adulthood. The immediate risk for this patient is intussusception.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is associated with hamartomatous polyps and an increased risk of intussusception in young patients.

 

 

Key Features of PJS:

 

  • Autosomal dominant syndrome
  • Mutation in STK11 (LKB1) tumor suppressor gene
  • Characterized by:
    • Mucocutaneous pigmentation (lips, buccal mucosa, fingers)
    • Hamartomatous polyps in GI tract (esp. small intestine)
    • Recurrent abdominal pain, melena

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following conditions does not show the graph as depicted by the red line: Sickle cell anemia Autoimmune hemolytic anemia Hereditary spherocytosis Thalassemia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1 and 4

 

The graph shown represents an osmotic fragility test, which measures the susceptibility of red blood cells (RBCs) to hemolysis in hypotonic solutions. The red line shows a significant right shift in the fragility curve, indicating increased fragility of red blood cells. This is typical of conditions like hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where the RBCs have increased susceptibility to osmotic lysis.

 

In hereditary spherocytosis, the red blood cells are more fragile due to the defective cytoskeleton, leading to a higher rate of lysis at higher saline concentrations. Similarly, in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, autoantibodies coat the RBCs, causing increased lysis when exposed to hypotonic solutions.

 

The conditions sickle cell anemia and thalassemia do not show this pattern. In sickle cell anemia, the shape abnormality of red blood cells is due to the sickle hemoglobin, which affects their ability to deform, but their osmotic fragility is not as significantly altered as in hereditary spherocytosis. In thalassemia, the primary issue is related to defective hemoglobin production, which results in ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis, but not the same increase in osmotic fragility as seen in hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Only 1: This option would suggest that only sickle cell anemia does not show the curve, but thalassemia also does not show this pattern.

 

Option B. 2 and 3: Both autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hereditary spherocytosis do show the increased osmotic fragility represented by the red curve, making this answer incorrect.

 

Option D. 1 and 2: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia does display this pattern, so this option is incorrect as well.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Conditions like hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia show increased osmotic fragility, while sickle cell anemia and thalassemia do not demonstrate the same fragility pattern.

questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with progressive exertional dyspnea is found to have elevated liver enzymes. A liver biopsy is performed and light microscopy of the tissue specimen after periodic acid-Schiff staining is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's dyspnea?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Inter-alveolar septa destruction

 

The patient’s dyspnea and elevated liver enzymes suggest α1-antitrypsin deficiency (AATD). This genetic disorder causes unregulated elastase activity, leading to destruction of inter-alveolar septa and panacinar emphysema in the lungs. Liver damage results from the accumulation of abnormal α1-antitrypsin proteins, which are PAS-positive on staining, as seen in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Intra-alveolar substance accumulation: Seen in pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, not AATD, and does not typically involve liver enzyme elevation.

 

Option C. Interstitial infiltration: Found in interstitial lung diseases but lacks PAS-positive inclusions or liver enzyme elevation.

 

Option D. Bronchial hyper-reactivity: Characteristic of asthma, unrelated to liver issues or PAS-positive findings.

 

Educational Objective:

 

α1-antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) leads to inter-alveolar septa destruction, causing panacinar emphysema and liver enzyme elevation due to protein accumulation.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman consults a doctor due to persistent malaise for five years and presents with high blood pressure. She passes away unexpectedly within a week. The autopsy reveals her kidneys' external and bisected appearance, as shown in images. Which of the following is not expected to be seen in this patent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Autosomal dominant with low penetrance

 

The image and clinical history describe a classic case of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD). This genetic disorder is characterized by the development of multiple fluid-filled cysts in both kidneys, leading to renal failure over time. The condition is associated with mutations in the PKD1 gene on chromosome 16 or the PKD2 gene on chromosome 4. ADPKD follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with high penetrance, meaning that individuals with the mutation are highly likely to express the disease phenotype.

 

The patient’s high blood pressure is due to cyst-induced compression of the renal parenchyma, leading to increased renin secretion and secondary hypertension. The bisected kidney images show the classic appearance of multiple large cysts, which are characteristic of ADPKD.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Colonic diverticulum: Colonic diverticula are frequently associated with ADPKD due to the widespread nature of the connective tissue abnormalities in this disorder. Patients with ADPKD often develop diverticula, which can lead to complications like diverticulitis.

 

Option C. Increased risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage: Patients with ADPKD are at an increased risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage, typically due to the presence of berry aneurysms in the cerebral arteries. These aneurysms can rupture, causing life-threatening bleeding.

 

Option D. Mitral valve prolapse: Mitral valve prolapse is another common extracranial manifestation of ADPKD. It occurs due to connective tissue abnormalities affecting the mitral valve, making it more prone to prolapse.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is a high-penetrance genetic disorder associated with multiple cysts in the kidneys, hypertension, colonic diverticula, an increased risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage from berry aneurysms, and mitral valve prolapse.

questions.stem: A man with a renal disease presents to the clinic with worsening fatigue and muscle weakness. Further studies reveal increased lipid peroxidation products and decreased glutathione levels in his blood. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely contributing to his ongoing cellular injury?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ferroptosis

 

The key clues in the question include increased lipid peroxidation products and decreased glutathione levels, which strongly suggest the presence of ferroptosis, a form of iron-dependent programmed cell death. Ferroptosis is distinct from other forms of cell death, such as apoptosis, necroptosis, or pyroptosis, because it is triggered by the accumulation of lipid peroxides due to defective antioxidant defense mechanisms, particularly involving glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4).

 

Glutathione is a crucial antioxidant that neutralizes free radicals and prevents oxidative damage to lipids. In conditions where glutathione levels are depleted, as seen in this patient, the activity of GPX4 is impaired, leading to excessive lipid peroxidation, which is a hallmark of ferroptosis. Iron, a transition metal, catalyzes the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), exacerbating oxidative damage and contributing to cell death.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apoptosis: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by DNA fragmentation, cell shrinkage, and caspase activation. While apoptosis is important in many forms of cellular injury, it is not associated with lipid peroxidation and decreased glutathione levels, as described in this case.

 

Option B. Necroptosis: Necroptosis is a caspase-independent form of programmed necrosis, usually triggered by signals that also promote apoptosis but occur when caspase signaling is inhibited. It involves receptor-interacting protein kinase (RIPK) signaling pathways, but it is not characterized by lipid peroxidation or glutathione depletion.

 

Option D. Pyroptosis: Pyroptosis is a type of programmed cell death associated with inflammation and is mediated by caspase-1, -4, -5, or -11. It is triggered by microbial infections and is associated with the release of inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), leading to fever and cell death. This mechanism is unrelated to the oxidative stress described in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, programmed cell death mechanism characterized by increased lipid peroxidation and reduced glutathione levels, leading to oxidative stress and cell damage.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with endometrial carcinoma. Her mother died of endometrial cancer at age 50, and her 42-year-old brother was recently diagnosed with colon cancer. You suspect a familial cancer syndrome. Which gene in this family is most likely to be mutated?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) MSH2

 

The family history described in the question, with multiple cases of endometrial cancer and colon cancer, suggests a diagnosis of Lynch syndrome, also known as Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC). Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, including MSH2 and MLH1. These genes are responsible for correcting errors that occur during DNA replication. A defect in these genes leads to microsatellite instability and increases the risk for various cancers, particularly colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.

 

In this case, the combination of early-onset colon cancer in the brother and endometrial cancer in both the mother and the patient is highly indicative of Lynch syndrome. The MSH2 gene is one of the most commonly affected mismatch repair genes in Lynch syndrome.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. WT-1: WT-1 is a gene associated with Wilms tumor, a type of kidney cancer typically seen in children, not adults with familial colon and endometrial cancers.

 

Option B. APC: APC gene mutations are linked to familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), another hereditary cancer syndrome that primarily leads to multiple colorectal polyps and an increased risk of colorectal cancer. However, FAP does not involve endometrial cancer, making this option less likely in this scenario.

 

Option D. BRCA1: BRCA1 is a gene associated with breast and ovarian cancers. While it increases the risk of certain cancers, including breast, ovarian, and sometimes pancreatic cancers, it is not commonly associated with colorectal or endometrial cancer, as seen in this family.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is associated with mutations in mismatch repair genes (MSH2, MLH1) and significantly increases the risk of colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with a palpable lump in her left breast with bloody nipple discharge. A core needle biopsy is performed, and histopathology reveals sheets of small, pleomorphic cells infiltrating the stroma with the formation of glandular structures. Which of the following is not true for her?

options.label: A
options.text: Diamino benzidine is used for brown color in IHC.

options.label: B
options.text: For a score 2 in IHC, Fluorescence in situ hybridization is indicated.

options.label: C
options.text: Under activity of CDH1 gene tends to be bilateral and multifocal.

options.label: D
options.text: Over expression of E cadherin has association with familial gastric cancer.

questions.answerText: Over expression of E cadherin has association with familial gastric cancer.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Overexpression of E-cadherin has an association with familial gastric cancer

 

This case describes a woman with a breast lump and histopathological findings consistent with invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC), the most common type of breast cancer. Several markers and genetic changes are involved in the diagnosis and prognosis of breast cancer. The CDH1 gene, which encodes the protein E-cadherin, plays a crucial role in cell adhesion and maintaining the architecture of epithelial tissues.

 

  • E-cadherin loss or underexpression is associated with certain types of breast cancer, such as lobular carcinoma, and with familial gastric cancer. It is the loss of E-cadherin expression, not overexpression, that is linked to familial gastric cancer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Diamino benzidine is used for brown color in IHC: True. Diaminobenzidine (DAB) is a chromogen commonly used in immunohistochemistry (IHC) to produce a brown color, indicating the presence of the antigen of interest.

 

Option B. For a score 2 in IHC, Fluorescence in situ hybridization is indicated: True. A score of 2+ in IHC for HER2/neu expression indicates an equivocal result. To confirm amplification of the HER2 gene, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is often performed to determine whether HER2 is truly overexpressed.

 

Option C. Underactivity of CDH1 gene tends to be bilateral and multifocal: True. Mutations or under expression of the CDH1 gene (coding for E-cadherin) are associated with lobular carcinoma, which is more likely to be bilateral and multifocal compared to ductal carcinoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Loss of E-cadherin expression, rather than overexpression, is associated with familial gastric cancer and certain breast cancer subtypes, such as lobular carcinoma.

questions.stem: Pick the incorrect statements about hemolytic anemia Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and high mechanical fragility Increased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemia Mentzer index helps in differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia Donath Landsteiner antibody is seen in cold hemolysin disease
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1 and 2

 

Let’s break down each statement:

 

  1. Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and high mechanical fragility: This statement is incorrect. Sickle cell anemia does not show high osmotic fragility. Instead, hereditary spherocytosis is known for high osmotic fragility due to the spherical shape of the RBCs, which makes them more susceptible to lysis in hypotonic solutions. Sickle cells, due to their abnormal shape, have high mechanical fragility but not osmotic fragility.
  2. Increased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemia: This statement is incorrect. Increased HbA2 is typically seen in beta-thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency anemia. In iron deficiency anemia, HbA2 levels may be normal or even decreased.

 

Other Options:

 

  1. Mentzer index helps in differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia: This statement is correct. The Mentzer index (calculated as MCV/RBC count) is used to differentiate between thalassemia trait (index <13) and iron deficiency anemia (index >13).
  2. Donath Landsteiner antibody is seen in cold hemolysin disease: This statement is correct. The Donath-Landsteiner antibody is an autoantibody associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), a form of cold hemolysin disease. It binds to RBCs at cold temperatures and causes lysis upon warming.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Sickle cell anemia does not have high osmotic fragility. Increased HbA2 is associated with beta-thalassemia, not iron deficiency anemia.
  • The Mentzer index is a useful tool to differentiate thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia.
  • Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a key finding in paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (cold hemolysin disease).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with a history of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease presents with abdominal discomfort and elevated blood pressure. Pick the true statements about her condition She may have a mutation in the short arm of chromosome 3 High risk of papillary carcinoma of the kidney Histology shows cells with perinuclear halo Cells have high glycogen and fat inside them
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Only 1 and 4

 

1. She may have a mutation in the short arm of chromosome 3: True. Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with mutations in the VHL gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 3 (3p25). This gene is a tumor suppressor, and its mutation increases the risk of various tumors, especially renal cell carcinoma.

 

4. Cells have high glycogen and fat inside them: True. Clear cell renal carcinoma, the type associated with VHL disease, is known for its cells containing large amounts of glycogen and lipids. These cells appear "clear" on histology due to the removal of lipids during tissue processing, hence the name clear cell carcinoma.

 

Other Options:

 

2. High risk of papillary carcinoma of the kidney: False. Patients with VHL disease are at increased risk of developing clear cell renal carcinoma, not papillary carcinoma. Clear cell renal carcinoma is the most common subtype in VHL disease and is characterized by cells with high lipid and glycogen content.

 

3. Histology shows cells with perinuclear halo: False. This feature is more characteristic of papillary carcinoma of the kidney, not the clear cell carcinoma commonly seen in VHL disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with mutations on chromosome 3, leading to a high risk of clear cell renal carcinoma characterized by cells with high glycogen and lipid content.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male presents with an enlarging mass in his left thigh. A biopsy of the mass reveals pleomorphic spindle-shaped cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, frequent mitotic figures, and areas of necrosis. IHC staining is positive for vimentin and negative for cytokeratin. The tumor cells demonstrate overexpression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). Which of the following characteristics is most closely associated with the behavior of this tumor?

options.label: C
options.text: Invasion of the basement membrane and metastasis

options.label: D
options.text: Cellular senescence due to telomere shortening

questions.answerText: Invasion of the basement membrane and metastasis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Invasion of the basement membrane and metastasis

 

The clinical and pathological features described in this case suggest a sarcoma, specifically a pleomorphic sarcoma. The tumor is positive for vimentin, an intermediate filament found in mesenchymal cells, which is typical for sarcomas. The spindle-shaped cells, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, frequent mitotic figures, and areas of necrosis all indicate an aggressive tumor.

 

The overexpression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is a critical feature in this tumor. MMPs are enzymes that degrade the extracellular matrix and basement membrane, allowing for tumor invasion and metastasis. MMPs are closely associated with tumor progression, enabling malignant cells to invade surrounding tissues and eventually spread to distant sites through the bloodstream or lymphatics.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tumor cell evasion of apoptosis: While evasion of apoptosis is a hallmark of cancer, the overexpression of MMPs is more directly related to invasion and metastasis rather than apoptosis evasion.

 

Option B. Decreased angiogenesis: MMPs are actually involved in increasing angiogenesis, not decreasing it. MMPs promote the formation of new blood vessels, which supply the tumor with nutrients and facilitate further growth and spread.

 

Option D. Cellular senescence due to telomere shortening: Cellular senescence refers to the process by which cells stop dividing due to telomere shortening. This is not related to MMP overexpression, which is linked more with aggressive tumor behavior like invasion and metastasis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Overexpression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is associated with increased invasion of the basement membrane and metastasis, which contributes to the aggressive nature of sarcomas.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not correct?

options.label: A
options.text: FISH is useful for chromosomal anomalies (like deletion, amplification, and translocation)

options.label: B
options.text: Single base primer extension is done for detection of point mutation

options.label: C
options.text: Array-based comparative genomic hybridization cannot be used if deletion is unknown detect deletion/amplification

options.label: D
options.text: Real-time PCR performed on cDNA is the method of choice for monitoring residual disease in CML

questions.answerText: Array-based comparative genomic hybridization cannot be used if deletion is unknown detect deletion/amplification
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Array-based comparative genomic hybridization cannot be used if deletion is unknown detect deletion/amplification

 

False. Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) is a powerful tool for detecting unknown deletions and amplifications across the entire genome. It does not require prior knowledge of the chromosomal region where the deletion or amplification might occur, making it useful for genome-wide analysis.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. FISH is useful for chromosomal anomalies (like deletion, amplification, and translocation): True. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is widely used for detecting chromosomal abnormalities, including deletions, amplifications, and translocations. FISH allows visualization of specific DNA sequences on chromosomes and is a powerful tool for identifying structural abnormalities.

 

Option B. Single base primer extension is done for detection of point mutation: True. Single base primer extension is a technique used to detect specific point mutations at known sites within the DNA. It involves the extension of a primer by a single nucleotide complementary to the base at the mutation site.

 

Option D. Real-time PCR performed on cDNA is the method of choice for monitoring residual disease in CML: True. Real-time PCR performed on cDNA, particularly targeting the BCR-ABL fusion gene, is the standard method for monitoring minimal residual disease (MRD) in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It is highly sensitive and specific for detecting low levels of disease post-treatment.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) can be used to detect unknown deletions and amplifications across the genome. Therefore, statement C is incorrect.

Ans. D) Cryo poor plasma: TTP

 

Cryo-poor plasma (also known as cryosupernatant) is used in the treatment of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Cryo-poor plasma lacks clotting factors like fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, which are retained in the cryoprecipitate, and is preferred in TTP because it helps replace ADAMTS13, the enzyme deficient in TTP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cryoprecipitate: hemophilia B: Incorrect. Hemophilia B involves a deficiency in factor IX, which is not present in cryoprecipitate.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male presents with vague abdominal discomfort and early satiety. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a 6 cm mass in the stomach. Endoscopic biopsy shows spindle-shaped cells with positive immunohistochemical staining for CD117 and DOG1. Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) NRG-1

 

Incorrect marker. NRG-1 (Neuregulin 1) is not associated with GISTs. It is involved in other biological processes, including cell growth and differentiation, but it is not a recognized marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. KIT: KIT (CD117) is a key marker in GIST. It is mutated in the majority of GIST cases and is used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

 

Option B. PDGFR: PDGFRA mutations are found in a subset of GISTs, especially in tumors that are KIT-negative. It plays a role in the development and progression of these tumors.

 

Option C. SDH: SDH deficiency is seen in a distinct subset of GISTs, often referred to as SDH-deficient GISTs. These tumors are typically seen in younger patients and often involve the stomach.

 

Educational Objective:

 

KIT (CD117), PDGFR, and SDH are common markers associated with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs). NRG-1 is not a marker for GIST.

questions.stemHtml: Physical examination of a 23 year old man diagnosed with chronic hepatitis shows corneal changes that are visible to the naked eye, as shown in the image. This patient is most likely to have which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Basal ganglia atrophy

 

The image shows a classic example of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which are golden-brown or greenish rings around the corneal margin. These rings result from copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea and are a hallmark of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). Wilson’s disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which is responsible for the transport of copper within liver cells, enabling copper to be incorporated into ceruloplasmin and excreted into bile. A defect in the ATP7B gene leads to copper accumulation in various organs, particularly the liver, brain, cornea, and kidneys.

 

Patients with Wilson’s disease often present with hepatic involvement (e.g., chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis) and neurological symptoms, particularly affecting the basal ganglia, leading to motor abnormalities like tremors, dystonia, and parkinsonism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pulmonary emphysema: Pulmonary emphysema is primarily associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and does not feature corneal copper deposition or Kayser-Fleischer rings.

 

Option B. Diabetes mellitus: Diabetes mellitus is not associated with corneal copper deposition or the findings seen in Wilson's disease.

 

Option D. Renal cancer: While Wilson’s disease can affect the kidneys, the specific corneal changes seen here (Kayser-Fleischer rings) are not linked to renal cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wilson's disease is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, which leads to copper accumulation in the liver, brain (especially the basal ganglia), cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), and kidneys.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a history of heavy menstrual bleeding, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental procedures. Her family history is significant for similar bleeding issues in her mother. Laboratory studies show a normal platelet count, prolonged aPTT as well as prolonged bleeding time. Platelet aggregation testing shows abnormal aggregation in the presence of ristocetin, but normal aggregation with ADP and collagen. Which of the following is the not an appropriate statement for her condition?

options.label: B

In von Willebrand Disease, Type I and Type III subtypes differ in severity:

 

  • Type I vWD is the most common form and usually presents with mild to moderate bleeding symptoms due to a partial quantitative deficiency of vWF.
  • Type III vWD, though typically more severe, may present with a variable range of bleeding symptoms, including mild bleeding episodes in certain cases, despite its usual association with severe bleeding. Therefore, the association of mild bleeding with Type III in certain atypical cases can justify this option in this context.

 

Since the patient has prolonged aPTT and abnormal ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, these findings align with a deficiency in von Willebrand factor.

Option D. Autosomal dominant variant has mild bleeding: Type I vWD (often autosomal dominant) usually presents mildly, but Type III is typically autosomal recessive and can vary in severity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In von Willebrand Disease, Type III is typically severe but may present with mild bleeding in certain atypical cases.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is an incorrect statement about the condition having cells as shown with an inflammatory background? The cells are of B cell origin and have CD30 + and PAX 5 +Commonest site affected is the Waldeyer ringNodular sclerosis variant commonly involves the mediastinum Lymphocyte predominant variant has poor prognosis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Only 2 and 4

 

The cells shown in the image are Reed-Sternberg cells, which are characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). Reed-Sternberg cells are large, often binucleate or multinucleate, with prominent nucleoli that give the appearance of "owl eyes." These cells are typically surrounded by a mixed inflammatory background, consisting of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and histiocytes.

 

2. Commonest site affected is the Waldeyer ring: Incorrect. The Waldeyer ring (a ring of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx, including the tonsils) is not the most commonly affected site in Hodgkin lymphoma. The cervical lymph nodes and mediastinum are more commonly involved, especially in the nodular sclerosis subtype of HL. The Waldeyer ring is more frequently associated with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

 

4. Lymphocyte predominant variant has poor prognosis: Incorrect. The lymphocyte-predominant variant of Hodgkin lymphoma generally has a good prognosis, especially compared to other subtypes. It has a more indolent course and tends to respond well to treatment.

 

Other Options:

 

1. The cells are of B cell origin and have CD30+ and PAX5+: Correct. Reed-Sternberg cells are of B-cell origin and typically express CD30 and PAX5. They may also express CD15. This statement is true.

 

3. Nodular sclerosis variant commonly involves the mediastinum: Correct. The nodular sclerosis variant of Hodgkin lymphoma often presents with mediastinal involvement. It is the most common subtype of HL and frequently affects young adults.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Reed-Sternberg cells are characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma, which commonly involves cervical lymph nodes and the mediastinum, not the Waldeyer ring. The lymphocyte-predominant variant of Hodgkin lymphoma generally has a good prognosis.

questions.stem: "Moldy" grains in some low socio economic area populated areas contain a substance that causes a specific G-to-T mutation in gene p53. The population in these regions is expected to be at an increased risk of which of the following diseases?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Liver cancer

 

The G-to-T mutation in the p53 gene is closely associated with exposure to aflatoxins, which are toxins produced by the mold Aspergillus species. These molds grow on grains and other crops stored in warm, humid conditions, which are common in low-income regions with poor storage facilities.

 

Aflatoxins, particularly aflatoxin B1, are potent carcinogens and have been linked to the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). Aflatoxin exposure leads to mutations in the p53 gene, a crucial tumor suppressor gene. This mutation impairs the ability of p53 to regulate cell growth and prevent cancer formation, thus increasing the risk of liver cancer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lung cancer: While lung cancer is linked to environmental toxins (e.g., smoking and asbestos), it is not related to aflatoxin exposure. Aflatoxins primarily affect the liver, not the lungs.

 

Option B. Infectious diarrhea: Infectious diarrhea is typically caused by pathogens (e.g., bacteria, viruses, or parasites), not aflatoxin exposure.

 

Option D. Pancreatic cancer: Although mutations in p53 can be implicated in various cancers, aflatoxin exposure is specifically linked to liver cancer, not pancreatic cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Aflatoxins, produced by molds found in poorly stored grains, are known to cause a specific G-to-T mutation in the p53 gene, increasing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer).

questions.stemHtml: Match the following cancers with the respective genes involved:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1-D, 2-C, 3-A, 4-B

 

  1. SDHB: Paraganglioma
    SDHB (succinate dehydrogenase subunit B) mutations are associated with paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas. These tumors are found in the adrenal glands and extra-adrenal paraganglia.
  2. K-RAS: Pancreatic carcinoma
    Mutations in the K-RAS gene are common in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. They are also found in other cancers, including colorectal and lung cancers, but are particularly frequent in pancreatic cancer.
  3. JAK2: Myeloproliferative neoplasm
    JAK2 V617F mutation is a hallmark of myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g., polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis). It causes constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.
  4. ALK: Adenocarcinoma of the lung
    ALK gene rearrangements (e.g., EML4-ALK fusion) are associated with adenocarcinoma of the lung. These rearrangements are seen in a subset of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), especially in younger patients and non-smokers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • SDHB is associated with paraganglioma.
  • K-RAS is commonly mutated in pancreatic carcinoma.
  • JAK2 is involved in myeloproliferative neoplasms.
  • ALK rearrangements are seen in adenocarcinoma of the lung.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following symptoms is least likely to be observed in a patient diagnosed with the flow cytometry pattern as shown in the image.

options.label: A
options.text: Acquired defect in hematopoietic stem cells

options.label: B
options.text: Increased susceptibility to C5b-9 induced damage

options.label: C
options.text: Thrombosis causes high rate of mortality

options.label: D
options.text: C5 inhibitor therapy is the treatment of choice

questions.answerText: C5 inhibitor therapy is the treatment of choice
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) C5 inhibitor therapy is the treatment of choice

 

The flow cytometry pattern in the image indicates paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a condition in which hematopoietic stem cells acquire a mutation in the PIGA gene, leading to a deficiency in GPI-anchored proteins like CD55 and CD59. This deficiency makes red blood cells more susceptible to destruction by the complement system, particularly through the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), resulting in intravascular hemolysis.

 

While C5 inhibitors (like eculizumab) are effective at reducing hemolysis by inhibiting the complement system, they are not the curative treatment for PNH. The curative treatment for PNH is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). C5 inhibitors are used to manage symptoms but do not cure the underlying defect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acquired defect in hematopoietic stem cells: This statement is true. PNH is an acquired defect in hematopoietic stem cells, and the mutation in the PIGA gene results in a deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins like CD55 and CD59. These proteins normally protect cells from complement-mediated damage, and their absence in PNH leads to hemolysis.

 

Option B. Increased susceptibility to C5b-9 induced damage: This statement is true. In PNH, the lack of CD55 and CD59 leads to increased susceptibility to the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which damages and lyses red blood cells.

 

Option C. Thrombosis causes high rate of mortality: This statement is true. Thrombosis is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in PNH. Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome) and thrombosis in other unusual locations are common complications in PNH patients, leading to a high mortality rate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

PNH is an acquired disorder of hematopoietic stem cells leading to complement-mediated hemolysis due to the absence of CD55 and CD59. While C5 inhibitor therapy is useful in managing symptoms, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative treatment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the storage temperature of blood components?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Platelet 22-26°C, RBC 2-6°C, FFP -30°C

 

Blood components need to be stored at specific temperatures to preserve their viability and function.

 

  1. Platelets are stored at 22-26°C (room temperature) with constant agitation. Storing them at colder temperatures, like 2-6°C, can damage them and reduce their functionality.
  2. Red blood cells (RBCs) are stored at 2-6°C. This temperature helps maintain their viability for transfusion and prevents hemolysis or other degradation over time.
  3. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is stored at -30°C or lower to preserve clotting factors and other proteins until it is needed for transfusion. This prevents degradation of coagulation factors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Platelets are stored at 22-26°C with agitation.
  • RBCs are stored at 2-6°C.
  • FFP is stored at -30°C or lower.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man suffering from persistent fatigue and lymph node enlargement visits the outpatient department. Examination of his peripheral smear reveals the image as shown. Pick the incorrect option.

options.label: A
options.text: Arises commonly from a Naïve B cell

options.label: C
options.text: Tumor cells have high-level expression of BCL2

options.label: D
options.text: Investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis is flow cytometry

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Commonest cytogenetic mutation is 13p deletion

 

The image and clinical presentation are indicative of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), a condition often seen in elderly patients. The smear shows smudge cells, which are characteristic of CLL. 

 

The most common cytogenetic abnormality in CLL is 13q deletion, not 13p. The 13q deletion is associated with a more favorable prognosis, while other cytogenetic abnormalities (e.g., 17p deletion) are associated with worse outcomes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Arises commonly from a naïve B cell: This statement is correct. CLL typically arises from naïve B cells or memory B cells. These cells are often positive for markers like CD5 and CD23, and the disease is associated with a clonal proliferation of these cells.

 

Option C. Tumor cells have high-level expression of BCL2: This statement is correct. BCL2, an anti-apoptotic protein, is overexpressed in CLL, which contributes to the resistance of the leukemic cells to apoptosis, allowing them to survive longer and proliferate.

 

Option D. Investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis is flow cytometry: This statement is correct. Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosing CLL. It identifies the clonal population of B cells expressing CD5, CD23, and other markers characteristic of CLL.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • CLL is a malignancy of naïve B cells that frequently presents in older adults.
  • The most common cytogenetic abnormality is 13q deletion, and BCL2 overexpression is a hallmark of CLL.
  • Flow cytometry is the investigation of choice for confirming the diagnosis of CLL.

questions.answerText: Immune complex deposition: hemolytic anemia is SLE patients
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Immune complex deposition: hemolytic anemia in SLE patients

 

Incorrectly matched. Hemolytic anemia in SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) is not caused by immune complex deposition but is instead due to autoantibodies targeting red blood cells, leading to Type II hypersensitivity. Immune complex deposition, characteristic of Type III hypersensitivity, is involved in conditions like glomerulonephritis or vasculitis in SLE, not hemolytic anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation: skin rash after wasp bite: Correctly matched. This describes a Type I hypersensitivity reaction, where IgE antibodies bind to mast cells and trigger degranulation upon exposure to the allergen (e.g., wasp venom), causing symptoms like a skin rash, urticaria, and anaphylaxis.

 

Option B. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity: penicillin induced hemolytic anemia: Correctly matched. Penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia is an example of a Type II hypersensitivity reaction, where penicillin binds to red blood cells, and antibodies (typically IgG) target these cells for destruction via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) or complement activation.

 

Option D. T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity: Contact dermatitis due to poison ivy: Correctly matched. Contact dermatitis from poison ivy is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction, where T cells mediate a delayed response, typically occurring 48-72 hours after exposure. This results in a localized skin reaction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity) is not responsible for hemolytic anemia in SLE; the hemolytic anemia in SLE is caused by autoantibodies (Type II hypersensitivity).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male with anorexia and fatigue is found to have persistently elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels. He is also positive for HBsAg. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of liver injury in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Viral cytotoxic effect and hepatocyte necrosis with following secondary inflammation

options.label: B
options.text: Antibody response to viral antigens on the cell surface with antibody-mediated cell damage

options.label: C
options.text: Circulating viral antigen-antibody complexes with small vessel deposition and immunologic vessel injury

options.label: D

questions.answerText: CD8+ T lymphocyte response to viral antigens on the cell surface resulting hepatocyte damage
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) CD8+ T lymphocyte response to viral antigens on the cell surface resulting in hepatocyte damage

 

The patient's positive HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) and elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST) suggest a diagnosis of chronic hepatitis B infection. In hepatitis B, the liver damage is primarily caused by the host’s immune response, not direct viral cytotoxicity.

 

  • The CD8+ T lymphocytes (cytotoxic T cells) recognize viral antigens expressed on the surface of hepatocytes (infected with the hepatitis B virus) via MHC class I molecules. These cytotoxic T cells attack the hepatocytes, causing inflammation and liver injury.
  • This immune-mediated damage leads to hepatocyte necrosis, which is reflected in the elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Viral cytotoxic effect and hepatocyte necrosis with following secondary inflammation: This is incorrect because the hepatitis B virus does not directly damage hepatocytes. Instead, the liver damage is mediated by the host’s immune system (via CD8+ T cells).

 

Option B. Antibody response to viral antigens on the cell surface with antibody-mediated cell damage: This is incorrect because the primary mechanism of liver injury in hepatitis B infection is mediated by CD8+ T cells, not by antibodies. Circulating viral antigen-antibody complexes with small vessel deposition and immunologic vessel injury: This is incorrect because this describes a Type III hypersensitivity reaction, such as those seen in conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). questions.stem: A 34-year-old female comes to your office for evaluation of infertility. She reveals that her menstrual periods occur 2-3 times per year. Physical examination reveals moderate obesity and excessive facial hair growth. This patient is at increased risk for which of the following conditions:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Endometrial adenocarcinoma

 

This patient has symptoms consistent with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), which is characterized by oligomenorrhea (infrequent periods), obesity, hirsutism (excess facial hair), and infertility. PCOS is associated with insulin resistance, which can lead to type 2 diabetes, and a hyper-estrogenic state due to an imbalance in FSH and LH. This state increases the risk of developing endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial adenocarcinoma due to prolonged, unopposed estrogen exposure.

 

  • Endometrial adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer that arises from the endometrium (lining of the uterus). Women with PCOS have an increased risk due to chronic anovulation, which leads to unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium without the protective effects of progesterone.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Diabetes mellitus, type 1: Incorrect. While patients with PCOS are at increased risk for diabetes, it is specifically type 2 diabetes due to insulin resistance, not type 1 diabetes, which is an autoimmune condition.

 

Option C. Adrenal atrophy: Incorrect. Adrenal atrophy is not typically seen in PCOS. This condition affects the ovaries, leading to hormonal imbalances, but the adrenal glands are not involved in causing the primary symptoms of PCOS.

 

Option D. Cushing syndrome: Incorrect. While Cushing syndrome can cause obesity and menstrual irregularities, it is not commonly associated with PCOS. PCOS is more commonly associated with insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism (excess male hormones).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) are at increased risk of endometrial adenocarcinoma due to prolonged unopposed estrogen stimulation. PCOS also increases the risk for type 2 diabetes due to insulin resistance, but not type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old female with a 1-week history of dysuria and flank pain develops chills, high fever, and confusion. Her blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg and her heart rate is 120/min. Her extremities are warm, and her breath is rapid and shallow. Which of the following substances is most likely responsible for the patient's current symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) TNF-α

 

This patient presents with dysuria, flank pain, fever, and hypotension, which are suggestive of urosepsis, a systemic infection likely stemming from a urinary tract infection (UTI). The symptoms of sepsis, including hypotension, fever, tachycardia, and confusion, result from a systemic inflammatory response due to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, the most important of which is tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α).

 

TNF-α is a potent pro-inflammatory cytokine produced primarily by macrophages in response to bacterial endotoxins (like lipopolysaccharides). It plays a key role in causing the fever, vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and hypotension seen in septic shock.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Leukotriene B4: Incorrect. Leukotriene B4 is involved in neutrophil chemotaxis but does not directly cause the systemic inflammatory response seen in sepsis. It is more associated with localized inflammation rather than the systemic effects of sepsis.

 

Option B. IL-4: Incorrect. IL-4 is primarily involved in the differentiation of T-helper cells and the stimulation of B-cell antibody production. It plays a role in allergic responses and is not responsible for the systemic inflammation seen in septic shock.

 

Option C. IL-10: Incorrect. IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that helps to regulate and suppress the immune response. It would reduce inflammation, not cause the symptoms seen in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

TNF-α is a critical mediator of the systemic inflammatory response in sepsis, leading to fever, hypotension, and shock. Its overproduction is responsible for the hemodynamic instability seen in septic shock.

Ans. D) A 50-year-old woman, with a long history of pruritus and fatigue who has pale stools and xanthelasma

 

The biopsy findings of lymphocyte infiltration and granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts are characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), an autoimmune disease that primarily affects middle-aged women.

 

PBC is characterized by chronic inflammation and granulomatous destruction of the small intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to bile stasis and cholestasis. Symptoms of PBC include:

 

  • Pruritus (itching due to bile salt deposition in the skin)
  • Fatigue
  • Pale stools (due to lack of bile in the intestines)
  • Xanthelasma (cholesterol deposits around the eyes) due to hyperlipidemia associated with cholestasis.

 

PBC is associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), and laboratory tests often show an elevated alkaline phosphatase level, a marker of cholestasis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A 30-year-old homeless man with fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice: Incorrect. This presentation is more consistent with acute viral hepatitis or alcoholic liver disease, not PBC. A biopsy in viral hepatitis would show hepatocellular damage, not granulomatous destruction of bile ducts.

 

Option B. A 35-year-old man with a long history of ulcerative colitis who has fatigue and an elevated alkaline phosphatase: Incorrect. This presentation is more consistent with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), which affects both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis. PSC shows a different histologic pattern, including onion-skin fibrosis around bile ducts rather than granulomatous inflammation.

 

Option C. A 50-year-old obese woman with fever and a prolonged episode of severe right upper abdominal pain after fatty meal ingestion: Incorrect. This presentation is more suggestive of acute cholecystitis due to gallstones, which causes inflammation of the gallbladder, not granulomatous destruction of bile ducts.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is characterized by granulomatous destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to cholestasis. It primarily affects middle-aged women and is associated with symptoms like pruritus, fatigue, and pale stools.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male treated for sinusitis with ampicillin later develops fever, maculopapular skin rash, and oliguria. His serum creatinine level is 2.5 mg/dL. Urine sediment microscopy reveals red blood cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils. The pathologic process in this patient's kidney most likely involves which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Renal interstitium

 

The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), which is commonly triggered by medications such as antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin). AIN is a type of hypersensitivity reaction that affects the renal interstitium, leading to inflammation. The classic findings in AIN include:

 

  • Fever
  • Maculopapular rash
  • Oliguria (reduced urine output)
  • Elevated serum creatinine (indicating acute kidney injury)
  • Urine sediment showing eosinophils, red blood cells, and white blood cells (especially neutrophils and eosinophils).

 

These findings support the diagnosis of drug-induced interstitial nephritis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Small renal arterioles: Incorrect. Diseases affecting the small renal arterioles (e.g., hypertensive nephropathy, thrombotic microangiopathies) would not present with the fever, rash, and eosinophiluria seen in this case.

 

Option B. Glomeruli: Incorrect. Glomerular diseases (e.g., glomerulonephritis) typically present with proteinuria, hematuria, and red blood cell casts, but they are not associated with eosinophils or drug hypersensitivity reactions.

 

Option D. Renal papillae: Incorrect. Diseases affecting the renal papillae, such as papillary necrosis, are typically associated with conditions like diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, or analgesic abuse, and they would not present with the eosinophiluria and fever typical of AIN.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction affecting the renal interstitium. It commonly presents with fever, rash, oliguria, and eosinophiluria.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to severe heartburn that is resistant to over-the-counter antacids. Physical examination shows scattered telangiectasias on the face, several ulcers at the tips of the fingers, and small calcium deposits in the soft tissues of the hands and elbows. Which of the following processes is the most likely cause of this patient's heartburn?

options.label: A
options.text: Abnormal location of the gastroesophageal junction

options.label: B
options.text: Fibrous replacement of the muscularis in the lower esophagus

options.label: D
options.text: Increase in resting lower esophageal sphincter tone

questions.answerText: Fibrous replacement of the muscularis in the lower esophagus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Fibrous replacement of the muscularis in the lower esophagus

 

This patient's presentation is suggestive of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), an autoimmune disorder characterized by widespread fibrosis of tissues, affecting various organs. Key findings supporting this diagnosis include:

 

  • Telangiectasias (dilated small blood vessels on the skin)
  • Ulcers at the tips of fingers (digital ulcers due to vascular insufficiency)
  • Soft tissue calcium deposits (calcinosis cutis)

 

The patient's heartburn is caused by fibrosis and atrophy of the smooth muscle in the lower esophagus. In systemic sclerosis, fibrosis of the muscularis propria leads to esophageal dysmotility and reduced peristalsis, especially in the lower two-thirds of the esophagus. This also results in lower esophageal sphincter (LES) incompetence, causing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which manifests as severe, refractory heartburn.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Abnormal location of the gastroesophageal junction: Incorrect. An abnormal location of the gastroesophageal junction (such as in a hiatal hernia) can cause GERD, but the presence of systemic findings such as telangiectasias and calcinosis suggests a systemic condition like scleroderma, not a structural abnormality like a hiatal hernia.

 

Option C. Increased gastric acid production: Incorrect. Increased gastric acid production can contribute to GERD, but this patient's heartburn is more likely caused by esophageal dysmotility due to systemic sclerosis rather than increased acid production.

 

Option D. Increase in resting lower esophageal sphincter tone: Incorrect. In systemic sclerosis, the opposite is true: the lower esophageal sphincter tone is decreased due to fibrosis, leading to reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus and heartburn.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy of Punjabi descent presents with fatigue and pallor. His physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies shows Hb 9.0 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, Red blood cell count: 4.2 million/mm³ and reticulocyte count: 2%. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Iron deficiency anemia

 

To differentiate between iron deficiency anemia (IDA) and thalassemia, the Mentzer index is used. The Mentzer index is calculated by dividing the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) by the red blood cell count (RBC). In this case, the Mentzer index is:

 

 

A Mentzer index >13 suggests iron deficiency anemia, whereas an index <13 suggests thalassemia. Since this patient's Mentzer index is 15, it strongly indicates iron deficiency anemia rather than thalassemia minor.

 

Key points supporting iron deficiency anemia:

 

  • Microcytic anemia: The MCV of 64 fL is below the normal range, indicating microcytic anemia.
  • Low RBC count: The RBC count of 4.2 million/mm³ is lower than expected for thalassemia, where the RBC count is typically higher.
  • Reticulocyte count of 2% indicates a low level of new red blood cell production, which is common in iron deficiency anemia due to the lack of available iron.

 

Although the boy is of Punjabi descent, a population at higher risk for thalassemia, the calculated Mentzer index suggests that this is more likely a case of iron deficiency anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anemia of chronic disease: Incorrect. This type of anemia is typically normocytic or mildly microcytic and is usually associated with chronic illness or inflammation. The low RBC count and lack of chronic illness in this patient make this diagnosis unlikely.

 

Option B. Thalassemia minor: Incorrect. Thalassemia minor typically presents with a lower Mentzer index (<13) and a higher RBC count. This patient's Mentzer index of 15 and lower RBC count are more consistent with iron deficiency anemia.

 

Option D. Sideroblastic anemia: Incorrect. Sideroblastic anemia typically presents with ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy, which is not mentioned here. It is also less common in this age group.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Mentzer index is a useful tool for distinguishing between iron deficiency anemia and thalassemia. In this case, the Mentzer index of 15 points towards iron deficiency anemia.

questions.stemHtml: A 5-month-old boy is being evaluated for poor weight gain since birth. He is noted to have bulky and greasy stools. A jejunal biopsy shows the findings seen in the image. This patient most likely suffers from which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Abetalipoproteinemia

 

The clinical presentation of poor weight gain, bulky greasy stools (steatorrhea), and a jejunal biopsy suggests a malabsorption syndrome. The most likely diagnosis in this case is abetalipoproteinemia, a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired synthesis of apolipoprotein B, which is required for the formation of chylomicrons and the transport of lipids from the intestine.

 

Key findings in abetalipoproteinemia:

 

  • Poor weight gain since birth due to malabsorption.
  • Bulky, greasy stools (steatorrhea) due to fat malabsorption.
  • Jejunal biopsy shows enterocytes with foamy cytoplasm, due to the accumulation of fat within the cells because it cannot be packaged into chylomicrons and exported.

 

Patients with abetalipoproteinemia also often have other features such as fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, including vitamin E deficiency, which can lead to neurological symptoms and retinal degeneration.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Celiac disease: Incorrect. Celiac disease typically presents later in life after the introduction of gluten into the diet. The biopsy in celiac disease shows villous atrophy and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, which is not consistent with the findings in abetalipoproteinemia.

 

Option C. Whipple disease: Incorrect. Whipple disease is a rare bacterial infection that usually affects adults and presents with malabsorption, arthritis, and other systemic symptoms. The biopsy in Whipple disease shows PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria, which is not characteristic of this case.

 

Option D. Crohn's disease: Incorrect. Crohn’s disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract. It usually presents later in childhood or adolescence and is characterized by transmural inflammation and granulomas on biopsy, which is not consistent with this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Abetalipoproteinemia is a rare inherited disorder that presents in infancy with poor weight gain, steatorrhea, and a biopsy showing foamy cytoplasm in enterocytes due to impaired lipid transport.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) after presenting with fever, pallor, and easy bruising. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 12,000/mm³, hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, and platelet count of 80,000/mm³. Flow cytometry reveals that the blasts are positive for CD10 and CD19. Which of the following is the most favorable prognostic factor in this patient’s case?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Hyperdiploidy (> 50 chromosomes)

 

In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), several factors influence prognosis. The presence of hyperdiploidy, meaning more than 50 chromosomes in the leukemic blasts, is associated with a favorable prognosis. Hyperdiploidy reflects a more responsive form of leukemia to treatment and is linked to higher remission and survival rates.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Age < 1 year: Incorrect. An age less than 1 year is associated with a worse prognosis in ALL. The best prognostic age range for ALL is between 1 and 10 years.

 

Option B. Presence of the Philadelphia chromosome (t[9;22]): Incorrect. The Philadelphia chromosome (t[9;22]) is associated with a poor prognosis in ALL, as it is linked to a more aggressive form of the disease.

 

Option D. Initial WBC count > 50,000/mm³: Incorrect. An initial WBC count greater than 50,000/mm³ is considered a poor prognostic factor in ALL, as it often indicates a more aggressive form of the leukemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the presence of hyperdiploidy (> 50 chromosomes) is a favorable prognostic factor, while other factors like age < 1 year, the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, and high WBC count are associated with a poorer prognosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is properly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: Anaphylaxis on blood transfusion: IgE deficiency

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase: SCID

options.label: C
options.text: Defective CD40L and CD40 interaction: hyper IgE syndrome

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow X ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome

questions.answerText: Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase: SCID
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase: SCID

 

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a genetic disorder characterized by a severe deficiency in both B and T cells. One of the causes of SCID is a deficiency in adenosine deaminase (ADA), which leads to the accumulation of toxic metabolites that impair lymphocyte development.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anaphylaxis on blood transfusion: IgE deficiency: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis during blood transfusion is more commonly associated with IgA deficiency, not IgE deficiency. Patients with IgA deficiency may develop severe allergic reactions to blood products containing IgA.

 

Option C. Defective CD40L and CD40 interaction: hyper IgE syndrome: Incorrect. A defective CD40L and CD40 interaction is the hallmark of hyper IgM syndrome, not hyper IgE syndrome. Hyper IgE syndrome (also known as Job syndrome) is characterized by elevated IgE levels, skin infections, and recurrent pneumonia.

 

Option D. Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow on X-ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome: Incorrect. While DiGeorge syndrome is associated with cardiac defects, hypocalcemia (not hypercalcemia), and an absent thymic shadow, it presents with hypocalcemia due to parathyroid hypoplasia, not hypercalcemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) can result from adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, leading to a lack of both B and T cells and profound immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60 fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) HbA2 levels

 

This patient presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia (low MCV, low hemoglobin) and an elevated RBC count (5.2 million), which is suggestive of thalassemia, particularly beta-thalassemia minor (trait).

 

To differentiate between iron deficiency anemia and thalassemia, the Mentzer index is often calculated:

 

 

A Mentzer index < 13 suggests thalassemia, while an index > 13 suggests iron deficiency anemia. In this case, the Mentzer index is 11.5, indicating thalassemia. The next best investigation would be to measure HbA2 levels to confirm a diagnosis of beta-thalassemia minor, where HbA2 levels are elevated (typically >3.5%).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serum ferritin levels: Incorrect. While serum ferritin is used to assess iron stores and diagnose iron deficiency anemia, the elevated RBC count and low Mentzer index suggest thalassemia, not iron deficiency.

 

Option C. Serum folate levels: Incorrect. Serum folate is measured to assess megaloblastic anemia, which presents as macrocytic anemia (increased MCV), not microcytic anemia.

 

Option D. Serum homocysteine levels: Incorrect. Elevated homocysteine levels are associated with vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, both of which cause macrocytic anemia, not microcytic anemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient with microcytic hypochromic anemia and an elevated RBC count, the Mentzer index can help differentiate between thalassemia and iron deficiency anemia. A Mentzer index < 13 points to thalassemia, and measuring HbA2 levels is the next best step to confirm beta-thalassemia minor.
