questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with complaints of fatigue, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss over the past three months. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 150,000/μL with a peripheral smear image as shown. Which of the following is not true about his condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Exhibits the phenomenon of oncogene addiction

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of a reciprocal translocation detected by FISH

options.label: D
options.text: Clinically may progress to acute leukemia

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Presence of increased LAP score

 

This patient presents with a constellation of symptoms, including splenomegaly, marked leukocytosis, and night sweats, which strongly suggests chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). The peripheral blood smear, with an elevated white blood cell count and a mix of immature granulocytes, is characteristic of CML.

 

Key findings and characteristics of CML:

 

  • CML is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome, a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22]), resulting in the BCR-ABL fusion gene. This translocation can be detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
  • The BCR-ABL fusion protein has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity, driving uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells. This is an example of oncogene addiction, where the cancer is dependent on the activity of the BCR-ABL oncogene.
  • CML can progress to a blast crisis, which is an acute leukemia transformation.

 

A hallmark of CML is a low or decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score, which helps to distinguish it from other causes of leukocytosis, such as leukemoid reactions, which exhibit an increased LAP score.

 

False. In CML, the LAP score is decreased, which helps distinguish it from benign causes of leukocytosis, such as infections or inflammatory conditions (where the LAP score is increased).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Exhibits the phenomenon of oncogene addiction: True. CML exhibits oncogene addiction due to the dependence on the BCR-ABL fusion protein for the malignant phenotype.

 

Option C. Presence of a reciprocal translocation detected by FISH: True. The characteristic t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome) can be detected using FISH, and it is a key diagnostic feature of CML.

 

Option D. Clinically may progress to acute leukemia : True. CML can progress to a blast crisis, transforming into acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • CML is associated with a low LAP score, the BCR-ABL fusion gene, and the potential to progress to acute leukemia.
  • The Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR-ABL translocation are hallmark features of CML and can be detected by FISH.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with an 8-year history of ulcerative colitis visits her physician because she is concerned about her risk of colon cancer. Her concern is precipitated by the recent death of one of her close family-friends from colon cancer. She has no other co-morbid conditions and is currently well-controlled with sulfasalazine. Compared to sporadic colorectal carcinoma, colorectal malignancy arising in this patient would most likely exhibit which of the following features?

options.label: C
options.text: Develop an early APC gene mutation

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Be multifocal in nature

 

This patient has ulcerative colitis (UC), which is a chronic inflammatory condition of the colon and increases the risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC). Colorectal cancer associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), such as ulcerative colitis, differs in its pathogenesis from sporadic colorectal cancer in several important ways:

 

  1. Multifocal in nature: Colorectal cancer associated with ulcerative colitis is often multifocal, meaning it can arise in multiple locations within the colon simultaneously due to chronic inflammation, as opposed to sporadic CRC, which typically arises from a single adenomatous polyp.
  2. Chronic inflammation and dysplasia: In UC-related colorectal cancer, the chronic inflammation predisposes the colonic mucosa to dysplasia, which can progress to cancer. Unlike sporadic colorectal cancer, UC-associated CRC may not develop from a typical adenomatous polyp.
  3. Early mutations: Sporadic colorectal cancers often develop through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, with early mutations in the APC gene. In contrast, UC-associated colorectal cancer often does not follow this pathway and instead progresses through inflammatory dysplasia, with mutations in other pathways such as p53 occurring early.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Arise from an adenomatous polyp: Incorrect. While sporadic colorectal cancer often arises from adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer in the setting of ulcerative colitis typically arises from dysplasia due to chronic inflammation, without the presence of adenomatous polyps.

 

Option C. Develop an early APC gene mutation: Incorrect. Sporadic colorectal cancer typically involves early APC mutations, but colorectal cancer associated with ulcerative colitis usually involves p53 mutations earlier, and APC mutations occur later, if at all.

 

Option D. Appear histologically low-grade: Incorrect. Colorectal cancer associated with ulcerative colitis often appears as high-grade dysplasia and tends to be more aggressive than sporadic forms of colorectal cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Colorectal cancer in patients with ulcerative colitis is often multifocal, arises from chronic inflammation and dysplasia rather than adenomatous polyps, and typically involves early p53 mutations rather than APC mutations. These cancers are also more likely to be high-grade and aggressive.

questions.stem: The phlebotomist needs to collect samples from a patient for various tests. Among the options provided, which sequence of blood collection for testing ensures that the sample remains uncontaminated, considering the additives present in the collection tubes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Light blue → Red → Lavender → Grey

 

In blood sample collection, it is essential to follow a specific order of draw to prevent cross-contamination between the additives present in different collection tubes. If not followed, the results of the tests could be compromised. The correct order of draw minimizes the risk of additive carryover and ensures sample integrity.

 

The correct sequence based on the additives is as follows:

 

  1. Light blue (Citrate tube): This tube is used for coagulation studies and must be drawn first to avoid contamination by other additives, especially clot activators or EDTA, which could interfere with clotting times.
  2. Red (Serum tube): These tubes are either plain or have clot activators but contain no anticoagulants. Drawing the serum tube after the light blue tube ensures that coagulation tests are unaffected.
  3. Lavender (EDTA tube): EDTA is a potent anticoagulant used for hematology tests (e.g., complete blood count). If drawn earlier, EDTA could interfere with coagulation or serum tests.
  4. Grey (Fluoride/Oxalate tube): This tube contains sodium fluoride, which inhibits glycolysis, and is typically used for glucose testing. It must be drawn last to prevent contamination with anticoagulants that could affect other tests.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of blood sample collection is Light blue → Red → Lavender → Grey, ensuring proper sample integrity and avoiding contamination by additives from different tubes.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and lower abdominal pain for the past two days. She has no significant medical history and is sexually active. A urinalysis reveals positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites without WBC casts. Which of the following is true about her condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cystitis caused by Escherichia coli

 

The patient presents with classical symptoms of cystitis: dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and lower abdominal pain. Cystitis refers to a bladder infection, and the absence of WBC casts (which are typically seen in pyelonephritis) rules out a kidney infection. Urinalysis showing positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites suggests a bacterial urinary tract infection (UTI), with nitrites being an indicator of Gram-negative bacteria.

 

  • Escherichia coli is the most common cause of uncomplicated cystitis, especially in young, sexually active women. It accounts for about 75-95% of UTI cases in this demographic. The production of nitrites from nitrate reduction is characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, making it the most likely causative agent.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cystitis caused by Staphylococcus saprophyticus: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a Gram-positive bacterium and a well-known cause of UTIs, especially in young, sexually active women. However, it does not produce nitrites, making it unlikely in this case where positive nitrites were detected on urinalysis.

 

Option B. Pyelonephritis caused by Proteus mirabilis: Pyelonephritis involves infection of the kidneys, and in such cases, WBC casts would likely be present in the urine. The absence of WBC casts and the absence of symptoms such as fever, chills, or flank pain indicate that this is not pyelonephritis. While Proteus mirabilis can cause UTIs, it more commonly leads to complicated UTIs and produces urease, which raises urine pH.

 

Option D. Cystitis caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae: Klebsiella pneumoniae is another Gram-negative bacterium that can cause UTIs. However, it is a less common cause of uncomplicated cystitis compared to E. coli and typically affects patients with underlying risk factors such as hospitalization or catheter use.

questions.stemHtml: What is the probable diagnosis for a patient with a midline neck swelling and histopathological findings as shown in the image. Which of the following is correct about this condition?

options.label: C
options.text: Poor association with MEN II syndrome

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Associated with RET/PTC gene translocation

 

The image and description of a midline neck swelling suggest the diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer and often presents as a painless, midline thyroid mass. It has specific histopathological features, such as Orphan Annie-eye nuclei (clear nuclei) and nuclear grooves, which are typically seen on biopsy.

 

Key points about papillary thyroid carcinoma:

 

  • RET/PTC gene mutation is commonly associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma, especially in cases following radiation exposure.
  • Papillary carcinoma primarily spreads via lymphatics and typically involves regional lymph nodes. Hematogenous spread is uncommon and seen more in follicular thyroid carcinoma.
  • Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a common and effective diagnostic tool for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
  • Papillary thyroid carcinoma has a strong association with MEN II (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type II), a syndrome involving medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism.

 

Correct. The RET/PTC gene translocation is commonly seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, particularly in cases related to radiation exposure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cannot be diagnosed by FNAC: Incorrect. FNAC is one of the most reliable diagnostic methods for papillary thyroid carcinoma and is commonly used in clinical practice.

 

Option B. High risk of hematogenous spread: Incorrect. Papillary thyroid carcinoma primarily spreads through the lymphatic system, not hematogenously. Hematogenous spread is more common in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

 

Option C. Poor association with MEN II syndrome: Incorrect. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is less associated with MEN II syndrome. However, medullary thyroid carcinoma is strongly associated with MEN II.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy, characterized by RET/PTC gene mutations, lymphatic spread, and characteristic Orphan Annie-eye nuclei on histopathology. It is effectively diagnosed by FNAC.

 

  • Classic Microscopic Features of PTC:
    • Papillary architecture – branching fibrovascular cores.
  • Nuclear features:
    • Orphan Annie eye nuclei – nuclei with empty/clear centers due to chromatin clearing.
    • Nuclear grooves – longitudinal nuclear indentations.
    • Intranuclear pseudoinclusions – cytoplasm invaginating into the nucleus.
    • Psammoma bodies – concentric calcified structures (not always present but highly specific).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the incorrect statement regarding Huntington's chorea?

options.label: A
options.text: Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome 4

options.label: B
options.text: It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder

options.label: C
options.text: There is loss of function type of mutation

options.label: D
options.text: There are abnormal repeats of CAG

questions.answerText: There is loss of function type of mutation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) There is loss of function type of mutation

 

Incorrect. This is the incorrect statement.  Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a gain of function mutation due to an expansion of CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4. The CAG repeats encode glutamine, and the expansion of these repeats leads to the production of an abnormally long polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein. This causes toxic protein aggregation in neurons, particularly in the caudate nucleus and putamen of the brain, leading to the symptoms of Huntington’s disease, such as chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome 4: Correct. The mutation in Huntington's disease occurs in the huntingtin gene located on chromosome 4.

 

Option B. It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder: Correct. Huntington's disease is classified as a trinucleotide repeat disorder, specifically involving repeats of the CAG sequence.

 

Option D. There are abnormal repeats of CAG: Correct. The mutation in Huntington's disease involves an abnormal expansion of CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene, leading to the disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Huntington’s disease is caused by a gain of function mutation involving an abnormal expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats on chromosome 4, leading to neurodegeneration.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of smoking for many years presents with hoarseness of voice and a lump in the chest radiograph. The IHC of the pulmonary mass was positive for INSM1. Which of the following is the most likely histological precursor lesion in this condition?

options.label: D
options.text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) No known pre-invasive phase

 

Correct. Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) does not have a well-established pre-invasive lesion and tends to develop rapidly without passing through a detectable in-situ phase.

 

INSM1 is a marker that is highly specific for neuroendocrine tumors, particularly small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Small cell lung carcinoma is a highly aggressive form of lung cancer that is strongly associated with smoking. Unlike other forms of lung cancer, such as adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, small cell lung cancer does not have a well-characterized pre-invasive phase.

 

The development of small cell lung cancer tends to be rapid and aggressive, often without passing through a detectable pre-invasive stage. This is in contrast to other lung cancers that have more well-defined precursor lesions (e.g., adenocarcinoma in situ or squamous dysplasia for adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, respectively).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adenocarcinoma in situ: Incorrect. Adenocarcinoma in situ is a precursor to pulmonary adenocarcinoma, not small cell lung cancer. It typically presents as a peripheral lung lesion, not a central mass.

 

Option B. Squamous dysplasia: Incorrect. Squamous dysplasia is a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma, not small cell lung cancer. Squamous cell carcinoma is also associated with smoking but follows a different pathogenesis.

 

Option D. Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH): Incorrect. While DIPNECH is a precursor lesion for typical and atypical pulmonary carcinoid tumors, it is not associated with small cell lung cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC), which is associated with smoking, typically does not have a known pre-invasive phase and tends to present as an aggressive, invasive cancer without a well-characterized precursor lesion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with increasing lower extremity edema over the past several weeks. Urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria, no hematuria, and oval fat bodies. A renal biopsy is performed, showing diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane on light microscopy, with a "spike and dome" appearance with special staining. Which of the following is the most unlikely finding of this patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Subepithelial deposits seen on electron microscopy

options.label: B
options.text: Subendothelial deposits seen on electron microscopy

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) as the antigen

options.label: D
options.text: IgG4 is the principal immunoglobulin deposited in most cases

questions.answerText: Subendothelial deposits seen on electron microscopy
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Subendothelial deposits seen on electron microscopy

 

The patient’s clinical presentation, including nephrotic syndrome (massive proteinuria, edema, oval fat bodies in urine) and the renal biopsy showing diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with a "spike and dome" appearance, is characteristic of membranous nephropathy.

 

In membranous nephropathy, there are subepithelial immune deposits between the glomerular basement membrane and the podocytes, which cause the characteristic spike and dome appearance seen on special staining and electron microscopy. These immune deposits are typically IgG4 and complement (C3). The M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) is often the antigen implicated in idiopathic membranous nephropathy.

 

Incorrect statement. Subendothelial deposits are characteristic of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), not membranous nephropathy. In membranous nephropathy, the immune deposits are located subepithelially, not subendothelially.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Subepithelial deposits seen on electron microscopy: Correct statement. The hallmark of membranous nephropathy is the presence of subepithelial immune deposits, which cause the "spike and dome" appearance on light microscopy with silver staining. These deposits are seen on electron microscopy.

 

Option C. Presence of M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) as the antigen: Correct statement. In idiopathic membranous nephropathy, autoantibodies against the PLA2R antigen on podocytes are commonly found and are a key feature of the disease.

 

Option D. IgG4 is the principal immunoglobulin deposited in most cases: Correct statement. In membranous nephropathy, the immune deposits are primarily composed of IgG4 and complement components (such as C3).

 

Educational Objective:

 

In membranous nephropathy, the immune deposits are subepithelial, and the condition is often associated with antibodies against the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R). The presence of subendothelial deposits is uncharacteristic of membranous nephropathy and more consistent with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN).

questions.stem: A known patient of Burkitt lymphoma undergoes chemotherapy, following which he develops tumor lysis syndrome. All of the following may be seen with tumor lysis syndrome except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypercalcemia

 

Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) occurs when large numbers of cancer cells die rapidly in response to chemotherapy or radiation, leading to the release of intracellular contents into the bloodstream. It is particularly common in rapidly proliferating cancers like Burkitt lymphoma. The syndrome can lead to various metabolic disturbances, but hypercalcemia is not one of them. 

 

Incorrect. In tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), calcium levels typically decrease rather than increase. The lysis of tumor cells releases large amounts of phosphate into the bloodstream, which binds to calcium, causing hypocalcemia. This results in low calcium levels (hypocalcemia), not high calcium levels (hypercalcemia). Hypercalcemia is not a feature of TLS and would be unusual in this context.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyperuricemia: Correct statement. Tumor cell lysis results in increased purine release, which is metabolized into uric acid, leading to hyperuricemia.

 

Option B. Hyperkalemia: Correct statement. Potassium release from lysed cells leads to hyperkalemia.

 

Option C. Hyperphosphatemia: Correct statement. Phosphate release from dying cells leads to hyperphosphatemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tumor lysis syndrome is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Hypercalcemia is not a feature of tumor lysis syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen in an elderly patient with ileal resection?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Microcytic hypochromic anemia

 

In patients with ileal resection, the primary issue is malabsorption of vitamin B12, as the terminal ileum is where vitamin B12 is absorbed. Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to megaloblastic anemia, which is characterized by macrocytic red blood cells, not microcytic. Therefore, microcytic hypochromic anemia is not seen in these patients, making option C the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reversible dementia: True. Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to reversible dementia. Cognitive changes can occur, but they may improve with vitamin B12 supplementation.

 

Option B. Nuclear cytoplasmic asynchrony: True. This is a characteristic finding in megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency. The nuclear maturation is delayed compared to the cytoplasm in red blood cell precursors, leading to large, immature red blood cells.

 

Option D. Romberg sign positive: True. A positive Romberg sign (difficulty maintaining balance with eyes closed) can be seen in B12 deficiency due to demyelination of the dorsal columns of the spinal cord, leading to sensory ataxia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Ileal resection leads to vitamin B12 deficiency, which causes megaloblastic anemia (macrocytic, not microcytic), reversible neurological symptoms, and can cause a positive Romberg sign.
  • Microcytic hypochromic anemia is more commonly associated with iron deficiency or chronic blood loss, not B12 deficiency.

questions.stem: What can be the mechanism by which the phagolysosome causes cell death in autophagy?

options.label: A
options.text: Is both intra and extra cellular

options.label: B
options.text: Can fuse with other organelles directly

options.label: C
options.text: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

options.label: D
options.text: It is a single membrane structure

questions.answerText: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

 

In the process of autophagy, a phagosome (or autophagosome) forms and engulfs damaged organelles or cellular components. This autophagosome then fuses with a lysosome to form an autophagolysosome, where the contents are degraded by lysosomal enzymes. This is a critical step in the degradation and recycling of cellular materials, and in cases of excessive autophagy, it can lead to cell death by overwhelming the cell’s ability to maintain homeostasis.

 

  • Phagolysosome formation involves the fusion of the autophagosome with the lysosome, which is key to the degradation process.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Is both intra and extracellular: Autophagy is an intracellular process that occurs within the cell. It does not involve extracellular mechanisms.

 

Option B. Can fuse with other organelles directly: While autophagosomes may engulf damaged organelles, they do not fuse with organelles directly. Instead, they fuse with lysosomes to form autophagolysosomes for degradation.

 

Option D. It is a single membrane structure: The autophagosome is a double-membrane structure, not single membrane. The double membrane is one of the distinguishing features of autophagosomes in the autophagic process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In autophagy, the autophagosome fuses with a lysosome to form an autophagolysosome, where cellular materials are degraded. This process is essential for the breakdown and recycling of damaged organelles and can lead to cell death if autophagy is excessive.

questions.stem: All of the following features are observed in pleomorphic adenoma except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Perineural invasion

 

Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign tumor of the salivary glands, most commonly found in the parotid gland. It is characterized by its mixed histologic appearance, consisting of epithelial and myoepithelial cells, and may show chondroid (cartilage-like) differentiation.

 

Here’s why perineural invasion is not typically seen in pleomorphic adenoma:

 

  • Perineural invasion is more characteristic of malignant tumors such as adenoid cystic carcinoma, not benign tumors like pleomorphic adenoma. While pleomorphic adenomas can recur or undergo malignant transformation (leading to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma), they do not typically show perineural invasion in their benign form.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Myoepithelial cells: True. Myoepithelial cells are a key feature of pleomorphic adenoma, contributing to the tumor’s mixed histology.

 

Option B. Keratin pearls: True. Keratin pearls are not typically a feature of pleomorphic adenomas. However, keratin-producing cells may be present in pleomorphic adenomas, though they are not as common as in squamous cell carcinoma.

 

Option C. Chondroid differentiation: True. Chondroid differentiation (cartilage-like tissue) is a hallmark of pleomorphic adenoma, contributing to its pleomorphic nature.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Perineural invasion is more characteristic of malignant tumors such as adenoid cystic carcinoma and is not a feature of pleomorphic adenoma, a benign salivary gland tumor.

questions.stem: An intracranial mass is removed from a 33-year-old male. The mass is composed of elongated cells that have regular, oval nuclei and demonstrate areas of dense and loose growth patterns. The cells show S-100 immunoreactivity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Schwannoma

 

The histological description of elongated cells with regular, oval nuclei and areas of dense (Antoni A) and loose (Antoni B) growth patterns is characteristic of a schwannoma. Additionally, S-100 immunoreactivity is a key marker for neural crest-derived tumors, such as schwannomas.

 

  • Schwannomas are benign nerve sheath tumors that arise from Schwann cells, which are derived from the neural crest. They commonly occur in the cranial nerves, particularly the vestibular nerve, where they are known as vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas).
  • S-100 positivity is a hallmark of schwannomas because Schwann cells express S-100 protein.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Meningioma: Incorrect. Meningiomas typically arise from the arachnoid cap cells and are not associated with S-100 immunoreactivity. Meningiomas often show whorled cell patterns and psammoma bodies histologically.

 

Option C. Metastatic lung cancer: Incorrect. Metastatic lung cancer is not typically S-100 positive, and the histological features described here do not align with metastatic carcinoma. Metastatic tumors generally do not show the characteristic Antoni A and Antoni B patterns.

 

Option D. Optic glioma: Incorrect. Optic gliomas are astrocytomas of the optic nerve and are not typically S-100 positive. They are more commonly associated with mutations in the NF1 gene (neurofibromatosis type 1) and show glial cell markers like GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Schwannomas are characterized by S-100 immunoreactivity, elongated cells, and alternating areas of dense (Antoni A) and loose (Antoni B) patterns. These features distinguish schwannomas from other intracranial tumors.

questions.stemHtml: An athlete collapsed suddenly and dies. His cardiac biopsy image is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

 

The cardiac biopsy image demonstrates features consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). HCM is characterized by:

 

  • Myocyte disarray: The cardiac muscle cells are arranged in a disorganized, chaotic pattern. This hallmark feature is a classic finding in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is seen in the provided image.
  • Sudden death in athletes: HCM is a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes due to ventricular arrhythmias, often precipitated by exertion.

 

In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM):

 

  • The interventricular septum is typically thickened, which can lead to asymmetric hypertrophy of the heart muscle.
  • As a result, the left ventricular cavity, particularly during systole, can take on a "banana-shaped" appearance due to the bulging of the thickened septum into the left ventricle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Incorrect. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by normal or reduced ventricular volume with decreased compliance, often due to fibrosis or infiltration. It does not usually show the myocyte disarray seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

 

Option C. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Incorrect. Dilated cardiomyopathy features dilated ventricles and systolic dysfunction. The histology shows myocyte hypertrophy with interstitial fibrosis but lacks the organized myocyte disarray seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

 

Option D. Cardiac tumor/myocarditis: Incorrect. Myocarditis can show inflammatory infiltrates, while cardiac tumors have varied histological features depending on the type of tumor. Neither typically presents with the myocyte disarray seen here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by myocyte disarray, and it is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

questions.stem: A child presented with leukocoria and an intraocular mass which on histopathological examination had the presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in the child?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Retinoblastoma

 

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It often presents with leukocoria (white reflex in the pupil), which is the most common presenting symptom. On histopathological examination, Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are a characteristic feature of retinoblastoma.

 

  • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes consist of tumor cells arranged in a circular pattern around a central lumen, and these are seen in retinoblastoma due to its neuroblastic origin.
  • Retinoblastoma is caused by mutations in the RB1 gene on chromosome 13 and can occur in both familial and sporadic forms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Melanoma: Incorrect. Melanoma can affect the eye, but it is more common in adults and typically involves the uveal tract (uveal melanoma). Melanomas do not show Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathology.

 

Option B. Lymphoma: Incorrect. Intraocular lymphomas are rare and usually present in older adults. Lymphomas do not form Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

 

Option D. Squamous cell carcinoma: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy that typically affects the surface of the eye (conjunctiva) rather than presenting as an intraocular mass, and it does not exhibit Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Retinoblastoma is a childhood intraocular malignancy characterized by leukocoria and the presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathological examination.

questions.stemHtml: A female patient with infertility presented to the clinic and underwent a karyotyping. What is the likely diagnosis in the karyotype shown?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Turner syndrome

 

The karyotype shown in the image suggests Turner syndrome, which is characterized by a 45, X karyotype (also called monosomy X). In this condition, one of the X chromosomes is missing, leading to a 45, X chromosome configuration.

 

Key features of Turner syndrome include:

 

  • 45, X karyotype: This is the most common finding in Turner syndrome.
  • Short stature, primary amenorrhea, and infertility are common clinical features due to ovarian dysgenesis.
  • Patients may also have webbed neck, shield chest, and cardiac anomalies (e.g., coarctation of the aorta).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Down syndrome: Incorrect. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) would show three copies of chromosome 21. The karyotype does not show this pattern.

 

Option C. Klinefelter syndrome: Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome occurs in males and is characterized by a 47, XXY karyotype. The karyotype here shows a missing sex chromosome, which is consistent with Turner syndrome, not Klinefelter syndrome.

 

Option D. Edward syndrome: Incorrect. Edward syndrome (trisomy 18) would show three copies of chromosome 18, but this karyotype does not show this abnormality.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Turner syndrome is characterized by a 45, X karyotype, leading to infertility and other clinical features.
  • This karyotype does not show trisomies or an extra X chromosome, ruling out Down syndrome, Edward syndrome, and Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in a patient with the image of chromosome 15 represented here?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Prader-Willi syndrome

 

The image of chromosome 15 shows a paternal deletion on one side and a normal maternal chromosome. This pattern is consistent with Prader-Willi syndrome, which is caused by the deletion or disruption of the paternal copy of chromosome 15q11-q13.

 

 

Understanding the key syndromes:

 

  • Prader-Willi syndrome is typically caused by the loss of function of genes on the paternal copy of chromosome 15 due to deletion or uniparental disomy (both chromosomes inherited from the mother). Clinical features include hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, developmental delays, and hypogonadism.
  • Angelman syndrome results from the loss of the maternal copy of the same region on chromosome 15 (15q11-q13). The image does not represent this, as it shows a deletion on the paternal chromosome.
  • VHL syndrome (Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome) is related to a mutation in the VHL gene on chromosome 3, not chromosome 15.
  • Edward syndrome (trisomy 18) is a chromosomal disorder involving three copies of chromosome 18, and is not related to abnormalities on chromosome 15.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by a paternal deletion on chromosome 15q11-q13, while Angelman syndrome is caused by a maternal deletion in the same region.
  • The image shows a paternal deletion, which is diagnostic for Prader-Willi syndrome.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the likely disease looking at the pattern of inheritance as provided in the image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

 

The pedigree suggests an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern. In X-linked recessive disorders, males are more frequently affected because they have only one X chromosome, and if it carries the mutation, they will manifest the disease. Females are usually carriers (heterozygous), and for them to be affected, both X chromosomes would need to carry the mutation, which is rare.

 

Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome:

 

  • Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder. This condition is characterized by a triad of symptoms: eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections due to immune deficiency. Since it's X-linked, males are affected, while females can be carriers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Wilson's disease: Incorrect. Wilson's disease is autosomal recessive, so it would affect both males and females equally, and the pedigree doesn't show this inheritance pattern.

 

Option C. Achondroplasia: Incorrect. Achondroplasia is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, meaning the disease would appear in every generation and affect both genders equally.

 

Option D. Leber disease: Incorrect. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) follows a mitochondrial inheritance pattern, which means it is passed down from mothers to all offspring, but males and females would be affected, and only females can transmit it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The pedigree shows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, which is consistent with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

questions.stem: An adult patient presents with tall stature, pigeon chest deformity, long arm span, lens dislocation, and cardiac defects. The likely defect is in which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Fibrillin

 

The clinical features described in this question (tall stature, long arm span, lens dislocation, and cardiac defects) are characteristic of Marfan syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene that encodes fibrillin-1.

 

  • Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of the connective tissue that affects the skeletal system (tall stature, long limbs, chest deformities), ocular system (lens dislocation), and cardiovascular system (aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse).
  • Fibrillin is essential for the formation of elastic fibers found in connective tissues, and defects in fibrillin lead to the connective tissue abnormalities seen in Marfan syndrome.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Elastase: Incorrect. Elastase is an enzyme that breaks down elastin, and while elastin is involved in connective tissue integrity, mutations in elastase are not associated with Marfan syndrome.

 

Option C. Collagen: Incorrect. Collagen is a key structural protein in connective tissues, and mutations in collagen genes can cause disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta, but the symptoms described (tall stature, lens dislocation) are not typically seen in collagen-related disorders.

 

Option D. Laminin: Incorrect. Laminin is involved in the basal lamina of cells, and defects in laminin are associated with muscular dystrophies and skin disorders, not the features described in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, leading to connective tissue abnormalities, including tall stature, pectus deformities, lens dislocation, and cardiac defects.

questions.stemHtml: Match the mode of inheritance with the disorder in the appropriate column:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1-D, 2-A, 3-C, 4-B

 

Let's break down the disorders and their modes of inheritance:

 

  1. Autosomal dominant: D. Myotonia dystrophica
    • Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by progressive muscle wasting and weakness.
       
  2. X-linked recessive: A. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
    • Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. It primarily affects boys because they have only one X chromosome, and the gene responsible (DMD) is located on the X chromosome.
       
  3. Autosomal recessive: C. Cystic fibrosis
    • Cystic fibrosis is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Both parents must be carriers of the defective CFTR gene for the child to have the condition.
       
  4. Mitochondrial: B. Leber’s disease
    • Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is inherited via mitochondrial inheritance, meaning it is passed down from the mother to all offspring, but only mothers can transmit it.

 

Matching:

 

  • 1. Autosomal dominant: D. Myotonia dystrophica
  • 2. X-linked recessive: A. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
  • 3. Autosomal recessive: C. Cystic fibrosis
  • 4. Mitochondrial: B. Leber’s disease

questions.stem: Which technique is most commonly used to identify autoantibodies in serum?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Indirect immunofluorescence

 

Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) is the most commonly used method to detect autoantibodies in serum, particularly in diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma, and autoimmune hepatitis. In this technique, a patient’s serum is incubated with a substrate (often tissue sections or cells) that contains the target antigen. If autoantibodies are present, they will bind to the antigens, and a fluorescently labeled secondary antibody is then used to detect the bound autoantibodies.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ELISA: Incorrect. While ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) can be used to measure specific autoantibodies quantitatively, IIF is the more commonly used technique for screening and detecting a broad range of autoantibodies, especially in systemic autoimmune diseases.

 

Option B. FISH: Incorrect. FISH (Fluorescence in situ hybridization) is used for detecting chromosomal abnormalities or gene mutations but is not commonly used for identifying autoantibodies.

 

Option C. Direct immunofluorescence: Incorrect. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is used to detect immune complexes (antibody-antigen) deposited in tissues (e.g., skin biopsies in autoimmune blistering diseases) but is not used to detect circulating autoantibodies in serum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) is the most common technique used to detect circulating autoantibodies in serum, especially in autoimmune diseases.

questions.stem: The thymus gland is specialized in identifying the molecules of the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) that are presented to it. It discerns whether these cells belong to the body's own or are of foreign origin. Which specific gene is accountable for this function?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) AIRE

 

Correct. AIRE plays a critical role in central tolerance by enabling the presentation of self-antigens in the thymus to developing T cells, preventing autoimmune reactions.

 

The AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene is responsible for promoting the development of self-tolerance in the thymus by facilitating the expression of a wide range of self-antigens. This allows developing T cells to be exposed to self-antigens, so any T cells that react strongly to these self-antigens can be eliminated. This process is crucial for preventing autoimmunity.

 

In the thymus, AIRE plays a key role in central tolerance, where T cells are tested to ensure they do not react to the body's own tissues. AIRE enables the presentation of various self-antigens to developing T cells, and those that recognize self-antigens are typically deleted, ensuring that the immune system does not attack the body's own tissues.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. NOTCH1: Incorrect. NOTCH1 is involved in T-cell lineage commitment and differentiation in the thymus but is not specifically responsible for distinguishing self from non-self antigens.

 

Option B. E2A: Incorrect. E2A is a transcription factor involved in lymphocyte development, particularly in B-cell maturation, but it is not directly involved in the process of self-tolerance in the thymus.

 

Option C. Rag 1/2: Incorrect. Rag1 and Rag2 are genes involved in the recombination of T-cell receptor (TCR) and B-cell receptor (BCR) genes, which is crucial for creating diversity in the immune response but not specifically responsible for recognizing self versus non-self.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The AIRE gene is crucial for inducing self-tolerance by allowing the thymus to present a wide array of self-antigens to developing T cells, ensuring that potentially auto-reactive T cells are eliminated before they can cause autoimmune disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not correct about TRALI?

options.label: A
options.text: Seen most frequently with fresh frozen plasma

options.label: B
options.text: Pathogenesis is explained by double hit hypothesis

options.label: C
options.text: Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature

options.label: D
options.text: Occurs usually within 6 hours of starting transfusion

questions.answerText: Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anti HLA antibodies of recipient against donor antigens is causative in nature

 

TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury) is a rare but serious complication of blood transfusion, leading to acute respiratory distress. 

 

This is false. In TRALI, it is the anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies from the donor that react with the recipient's leukocytes, not the other way around. These donor antibodies activate neutrophils in the recipient’s lungs, leading to lung injury. So, this statement is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Seen most frequently with fresh frozen plasma: This is true. TRALI is most commonly associated with transfusions of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelets, as these components often contain plasma proteins and antibodies that can cause TRALI.

 

Option B. Pathogenesis is explained by double hit hypothesis: This is true. The pathogenesis of TRALI is described by the double-hit hypothesis, where the first hit is the underlying condition of the patient (such as inflammation), and the second hit involves transfusion of blood products containing anti-leukocyte antibodies or biologically active lipids that trigger an immune response in the lungs.

 

Option D. Occurs usually within 6 hours of starting transfusion: This is true. TRALI typically occurs within 6 hours of the initiation of a blood transfusion, often presenting with acute respiratory distress and hypoxemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

TRALI is caused by donor antibodies (such as anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies) reacting with the recipient's leukocytes, leading to acute lung injury. This makes Option C the incorrect statement, as it describes the reverse of the actual mechanism.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following microscopic finding with the type of tumor:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b

 

  1. Schillar Duvel bodies: These are seen in yolk sac tumors (endodermal sinus tumors), which are germ cell tumors. Schillar-Duvel bodies are distinctive microscopic features characterized by a central blood vessel surrounded by tumor cells in a cystic space.
  2. Presence of teeth, hair, cartilage, etc.: This is characteristic of teratomas, which are germ cell tumors that can contain elements from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm), often including tissues like teeth, hair, and cartilage.
  3. Signet ring cells: These cells are associated with Krukenberg tumors, which are metastatic tumors, often originating from gastric cancer, characterized by mucin-filled signet ring cells.
  4. Call Exner bodies: These structures are seen in granulosa cell tumors of the ovary. Call-Exner bodies are small follicle-like structures filled with eosinophilic material, surrounded by granulosa cells.

 

Matched Answer:

 

1. Schillar Duvel bodies: c. Yolk sac tumor
2. Presence of teeth, hair, cartilage, etc.: d. Teratoma
3. Signet ring cells: a. Krukenberg tumor
4. Call Exner bodies: b. Granulosa cell tumor

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: Which statement is not true regarding Crohn's disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Continuous lesion visualized in endoscopy

 

In Crohn's disease, the lesions are characteristically "skip lesions", meaning they are discontinuous, with patches of healthy tissue between areas of inflammation. This is in contrast to ulcerative colitis, where the inflammation is typically continuous and starts at the rectum, extending proximally without skipping areas.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rectum is not involved: True. Crohn's disease typically spares the rectum, unlike ulcerative colitis, which almost always involves the rectum.

 

Option C. Non caseating granulomas: True. Non-caseating granulomas are a hallmark of Crohn's disease and are found in about 50% of cases.

 

Option D. Cobblestone appearance: True. The mucosa in Crohn's disease often has a cobblestone appearance due to the patchy nature of inflammation and ulceration interspersed with normal tissue.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Crohn's disease is characterized by discontinuous ("skip") lesions, non-caseating granulomas, and a cobblestone appearance on endoscopy. Continuous lesions are not a feature of Crohn's disease, but rather of ulcerative colitis.

questions.stem: A woman diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome has undergone a renal biopsy. All of the following statement(s) is/are true except: FSGS is not diagnosed by a percutaneous renal biopsy.Patient should be observed for 24 hours following biopsy.Dark red clots in the urine following a biopsy indicate a hematoma.Patients with features of systemic amyloidosis and renal involvement should undergo renal biopsy.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 4

 

1. FSGS is not diagnosed by a percutaneous renal biopsy: Incorrect. This statement is false because focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is indeed diagnosed by a percutaneous renal biopsy. Renal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing FSGS, as it allows for histological examination of the kidney tissue to identify the segmental scarring of glomeruli, which characterizes FSGS.

 

4. Patients with features of systemic amyloidosis and renal involvement should undergo renal biopsy: Incorrect. While a renal biopsy can show amyloid deposits in the kidney, it is not always necessary in patients with systemic amyloidosis. Diagnosis of amyloidosis can often be made using less invasive methods, such as abdominal fat pad aspiration, which can reveal amyloid deposits without needing to resort to a renal biopsy. Therefore, this statement is false.

 

Other Options:

 

2. Patient should be observed for 24 hours following biopsy : True. After a renal biopsy, it is standard practice to observe the patient for complications such as bleeding. The patient should be monitored for 24 hours to ensure that no significant complications, such as hematuria or hematoma formation, occur.

 

3. Dark red clots in the urine following a biopsy indicate a hematoma : True. It is not uncommon to have hematuria (blood in the urine) after a renal biopsy, but the presence of dark red clots in the urine may suggest a hematoma (localized bleeding outside of blood vessels), which needs close monitoring and possibly further intervention.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • FSGS is diagnosed by percutaneous renal biopsy.
  • Renal biopsy is not always necessary in systemic amyloidosis; less invasive techniques like fat pad aspiration can be used.
  • After a renal biopsy, the patient should be observed for 24 hours for complications.
  • Dark red clots in urine following a biopsy could indicate a hematoma.

questions.stem: What is the most common genetic factor responsible for hypercoagulability?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Factor V Leiden mutation

 

The Factor V Leiden mutation is the most common genetic cause of inherited hypercoagulability. It is a mutation in the Factor V gene that makes the clotting factor resistant to degradation by activated protein C. This resistance leads to an increased risk of thrombosis because the clotting process is not properly regulated.

 

  • Factor V Leiden mutation is particularly associated with an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Protein C deficiency: Incorrect. Protein C deficiency can cause hypercoagulability, but it is much less common than Factor V Leiden mutation.

 

Option C. Antithrombin III deficiency: Incorrect. Antithrombin III deficiency is a rarer cause of inherited hypercoagulability, leading to unregulated clot formation, but it is not as common as Factor V Leiden mutation.

 

Option D. G20210A prothrombin gene mutation: Incorrect. The G20210A prothrombin gene mutation can lead to increased levels of prothrombin, promoting clot formation, but it is less common than Factor V Leiden mutation as a cause of hypercoagulability.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Factor V Leiden mutation is the most common genetic cause of inherited hypercoagulability, leading to an increased risk of thrombosis due to resistance to degradation by activated protein C.
  • Caused by a point mutation in the Factor V gene (G1691A).
  • Leads to a glutamine substitution at position 506 (Arg506Gln), making Factor V resistant to inactivation by activated Protein C.
  • Result: Prolonged procoagulant activity → ↑ risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE).
  • Inheritance:
    • Heterozygotes: 5–7× increased VTE risk.
    • Homozygotes: Up to 80× increased VTE risk.
    • Factor V Leiden is tested in young patients with unprovoked DVT or PE, or in those with family history of clots.
    • It does not affect PT or aPTT, so coagulation studies may be normal.
    • Acquired thrombophilias (like antiphospholipid syndrome) should also be considered in the differential.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following cell types and the malignancy they are associated with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

 

Let's review each of the cell types and the corresponding malignancies:

 

  1. Popcorn cell:
    • Correct match: b (Lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma)
    • The popcorn cell (also called LP cell) is a variant of Reed-Sternberg cells and is seen in lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma).
  2. Faggot cell:
    • Correct match: a (Acute promyelocytic leukemia)
    • Faggot cells are characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). These are blast cells filled with bundles of Auer rods.
  3. Cerebriform nuclei:
    • Correct match: d (Sezary syndrome)
    • Cerebriform nuclei are seen in Sezary syndrome, which is a leukemic phase of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides). The characteristic appearance of the nucleus resembles the folds of the brain.
  4. Starry sky:
    • Correct match: c (Burkitt lymphoma)
    • The starry sky pattern is a classic histological finding in Burkitt lymphoma, characterized by macrophages phagocytizing apoptotic cells, creating a starry appearance amidst the lymphocyte proliferation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Popcorn cells are seen in lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma.
  • Faggot cells are associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).
  • Cerebriform nuclei are characteristic of Sezary syndrome.
  • Starry sky pattern is a hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma.

 

Thus, the correct answer is A. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c.

questions.stem: Due to which phenomenon do B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Alternative RNA splicing

 

B cells express IgM and IgD simultaneously on their surface during early stages of development. This occurs due to alternative RNA splicing of the same heavy chain transcript. Both IgM and IgD share the same variable region for antigen specificity, but the constant region differs due to alternative splicing of the mRNA, allowing for the co-expression of these two isotypes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Somatic hypermutation: This process occurs later, primarily in germinal centers, and introduces point mutations into the variable region of the antibody genes to increase affinity for the antigen. It does not explain the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Option C. Affinity maturation: This process involves the selection of B cells that produce antibodies with higher affinity for the antigen after somatic hypermutation. It does not play a role in the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Option D. Allelic exclusion: This process ensures that B cells express a single heavy chain and a single light chain allele, leading to the production of one type of antibody with a specific antigen-binding site. It ensures monospecificity of B cell receptors, but it is not related to the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD on B cells is due to alternative RNA splicing of the heavy chain gene, allowing both isotypes to be produced from the same primary transcript.

questions.stem: A 60-day female infant presented with recurrent bacterial infections and suspected developmental delay. Extensive screening was performed, and a defect in the CD18 gene resulted in deficient beta-2 integrins. Which of the following steps of inflammation could be severely affected in this infant?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Adhesion

 

The defect in the CD18 gene, which leads to deficient beta-2 integrins, is characteristic of Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type 1 (LAD-1). Beta-2 integrins (such as LFA-1) are crucial for the adhesion step in the process of leukocyte migration to sites of inflammation.

 

In normal inflammation, leukocytes (white blood cells) adhere to the endothelium (lining of blood vessels) before transmigrating to sites of infection or injury. This adhesion is mediated by integrins, such as beta-2 integrins. Without functional beta-2 integrins (due to CD18 gene mutation), the adhesion step is severely impaired, preventing leukocytes from properly reaching the site of infection, which leads to recurrent infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Opsonization: Incorrect. Opsonization is the process where pathogens are coated with antibodies or complement proteins to enhance phagocytosis. This step is not directly affected by beta-2 integrin deficiency.

 

Option C. Margination: Incorrect. Margination refers to the movement of leukocytes toward the endothelial surface in response to inflammation. It precedes adhesion but does not involve beta-2 integrins.

 

Option D. Rolling: Incorrect. Rolling is mediated by selectins on endothelial cells and leukocytes, not integrins. Thus, rolling would not be affected by beta-2 integrin deficiency.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • A defect in the CD18 gene, which affects beta-2 integrins, primarily impacts the adhesion step of leukocyte migration during inflammation, leading to Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD) and recurrent bacterial infections.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe gastrointestinal bleeding. He has a history of cirrhosis secondary to chronic alcohol use. Initial laboratory tests reveal a hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL, platelet count of 60,000/mm³, and an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2.5. Despite transfusion with packed red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma, bleeding continues. Thromboelastography (TEG) results show a prolonged R-time, a normal alpha angle, a normal maximum amplitude, and a normal lysis index. Which of the following therapies is most appropriate based on these TEG findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fresh frozen plasma

 

In this case, the patient's prolonged R-time on thromboelastography (TEG) indicates a deficiency in coagulation factors. The R-time reflects the time it takes for clot formation to begin, and a prolonged R-time suggests that the patient has a coagulation factor deficiency, which is common in patients with cirrhosis because the liver is responsible for producing most clotting factors.

 

  • Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contains all of the coagulation factors and is used to treat coagulation factor deficiencies. Since the patient has already received FFP, another transfusion would be the most appropriate therapy to correct the clotting deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Platelet transfusion: Incorrect. The patient's platelet count is low (60,000/mm³), but the TEG results show a normal maximum amplitude (MA), which indicates that platelet function is normal. Thus, a platelet transfusion is not necessary based on these findings.

 

Option B. Cryoprecipitate: Incorrect. Cryoprecipitate is used to replace fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and Factor VIII, but the alpha angle (which reflects fibrin formation) is normal in this patient. Therefore, cryoprecipitate is not needed.

 

Option D. Antifibrinolytics: Incorrect. The normal lysis index on TEG indicates that fibrinolysis (breakdown of clots) is not a problem in this patient, so antifibrinolytic therapy is not required.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • A prolonged R-time on TEG suggests a coagulation factor deficiency, and the most appropriate therapy in this setting is fresh frozen plasma (FFP) to replenish these factors, especially in a patient with cirrhosis.
